chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Dialect and the th sound
summary: Hinton cites John Hendricks on dialect; Maxwell notes most languages lack th.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: So very descriptive. I know the great black jazz poet, John Hendricks, he has some tremendous expressions like that. He compares a West Indian black and a Caribbean black to an American black in a song which he sings, 'If you have a ship and you needed some rum, then you would stop at the Islands. So some stopped on the way to trade some slaves for some rum,' and he says, some stopped on the way, and the rest came on to the U.S.A. So some of the West Indians, some of the Caribbean slaves, were sold for rum, and the rest were brought onto the U.S.A. And he says, the ones in the U.S.A, they had to use a new language, so they got as close as they
could, so they say 'dis for this, and dat for that. And he says, it was pretty good for that saying.

Well, so does any European, because most people in the world don't have the th sound. They say Tee in their language where we say th. So when they try to say th they say tat, or Germans say dat, because that's the way they say it. So blacks are not the only ones. There are only two languages in the world, English and Icelandic, I think, that say th. So the rest of the word says tis and tat.
